title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). The preregistered design (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) used gpt-5-mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes), and shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions). Confirmatory outcomes (archived artifacts) show complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples); Cohen's h = 0.0. We explicitly state that two preregistered design choices—shared_initial_generation semantics and reuse of the same deterministic validator as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer—produced a deterministic ceiling effect in this run that rendered the primary estimand uninformative for assessing generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics. We present artifact‑grounded execution and analysis, diagnose why the design produced a null outcome, report representative task difficulty diagnostics, and give concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden future benchmarks so they expose generator×guard interactions.

sections.introduction:
Generative language models are increasingly applied to intent→configuration tasks in network operations (NetOps) because they can convert operator intent into device configuration sequences and staged change workflows (canaries, progressive rollouts, rollbacks). Prior studies demonstrate that LLMs can synthesize syntactically plausible configurations in controlled settings but emphasize that operational safety depends on the end‑to‑end pipeline—generation variability, deterministic verification, staged‑rollout semantics, repair procedures, rollback instrumentation, and provenance. To probe whether adding a deterministic runtime verifier meaningfully changes end‑to‑end safety outcomes we preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) on ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1.

Research question. Under ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1, does integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline); design and analysis were frozen prior to execution.

Contributions and high‑level result. We provide (1) a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 with all execution and analysis artifacts archived; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis showing that preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics plus reuse of a single deterministic validator produced a deterministic ceiling (universal acceptance) that made the primary estimand uninformative in this run; and (3) concrete, implementable benchmark‑hardening recommendations (independent generation, heterogeneous scorers, adversarial seeding, difficulty stratification) grounded in recorded validator traces and execution accounting.
sections.related_work:
We positioned this study at the intersection of intent‑to‑configuration translation, verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair architectures, and action‑aware evaluation. Recent intent‑based NetOps and IaC studies (intent→configuration pipelines, PreConfig, GraphSynth) show that LLMs can synthesize usable configuration templates in curated settings; verifier‑guided loops in IaC (e.g., TerraFormer) report correctness gains when verifiers inform repair or model updates. Deterministic network verifiers and reachability tools (header‑space style and Kubernetes reachability) effectively detect configuration errors offline, but their runtime integration in agentic pipelines and the evaluation of blocking/rollback semantics remain underexplored.

Agentic/tool‑augmented LLM architectures (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestrations) extend AIOps and RCA capabilities but introduce failure modes—hallucination, misapplied tools, and miscalibrated confidence—that motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployments. Several surveys identify an evaluation gap: community‑standard action‑aware benchmarks that combine generation, runtime blocking, staged rollouts, repair, rollback, and provenance are limited. Our experiment operationalizes a compact action‑aware staging benchmark under a strict preregistered design to probe runtime verifier utility and to surface concrete hardening steps.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory estimand. The study preregistration (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) fixed a paired binary confirmatory design with exactly N=400 tasks and the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline estimand. The analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 implemented the preregistered permutation‑based paired difference test (two‑sided, α=0.05) and an exact McNemar two‑sided test as corroboration. Bootstrap percentile CIs (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) were frozen for secondary summaries.

Adapter semantics and shared generation. The hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family was used with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer. Crucially, the preregistered adapter semantics set shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false): one deterministic LLM generation was requested per task and that identical candidate was delivered to both the baseline and guarded episodes. This design isolated validator acceptance behavior on identical strings rather than exposing independent generator variance. Model call accounting reflects this design: planned episodes = 800 (two episodes per task) while model_calls_used = 400 (one shared LLM call per task); execution artifacts record this mapping.

Episode flow, validator policy, and repair rules. For each task the adapter: (a) requested a shared initial candidate from gpt‑5‑mini; (b) delivered it to both baseline and guarded episodes; (c) in the guarded episode deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applied full intent‑constraint validation and—per the preregistered repair policy—could invoke up to one repair attempt. The runtime guard recorded validator_trace entries that include repair_applied flags, normalized_configuration, validation_before/after states, difficulty metadata, and the final validity decision. In this execution repair_applied = false for all episodes.

Deterministic replay and exclusion rules. The preregistration required deterministic three‑replay consistency checks: each agent+simulator pair was replayed three times and tasks with non‑identical replay outcomes or simulator errors would be flagged and excluded from primary analysis. The missingness plan mandated automated exclusion without human adjudication. In this run all deterministic consistency checks passed and no exclusions were applied.

Task generation and difficulty labeling. Tasks were deterministically produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and include fine‑grained difficulty metadata fields: changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, pattern, required_command_count, and level ∈ {medium, hard, very_hard}. Representative entries in the archived manifest show medium, hard, and very_hard patterns among early tasks; the full per‑task metadata for N=400 is archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl for auditors to aggregate.

Statistical procedures and contingency accounting. The primary analysis compares paired binary safe‑deploy outcomes per task (guarded vs baseline). The preregistered permutation‑based paired difference test (two‑sided) yields an exact permutation p‑value; McNemar’s exact two‑sided test is reported for concordance checking. Bootstrap percentile CIs for secondary continuous metrics use seed = 1729 and 10,000 resamples, as frozen in the preregistration.

sections.discussion:
Deterministic ceiling: proximate causes and interpretation. Two preregistered design choices combined to produce the deterministic ceiling: (A) shared_initial_generation delivered identical generator outputs to both conditions, intentionally isolating validator acceptance on identical strings; and (B) the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). When a deterministic verifier accepts the identical shared candidate, both conditions must yield identical safe‑deploy outcomes and the paired effect is necessarily zero. Hence the observed null result is a design artifact rather than general evidence that verifiers are unnecessary.

Power rationale invalidation and consequences. The preregistered power rationale assumed non‑ceiling baseline rates and intra‑pair variability allowing detection of an ≈10 percentage‑point difference with N=400. The universal acceptance observed invalidates those assumptions and collapses inferential uncertainty: the permutation and McNemar tests correctly return p = 1.0, but no inference about generator×guard closed‑loop interactions is possible from this run. Future designs must preserve baseline error rates or introduce controlled perturbations to maintain testable signal.

Artifact‑grounded benchmark‑hardening recommendations. Drawing directly from archived validator_trace structure and execution accounting we recommend these implementable steps for future preregistered runs: (1) independent per‑condition generation (independent_condition_generation = true) so each condition receives an independently sampled generator output, exposing generator variance; (2) separate runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer implementations (or independent scorers) to avoid conflating acceptance and scoring; (3) controlled adversarial seeding (preregister a fraction of perturbation seeds) to guarantee measurable baseline failure rates; (4) difficulty‑stratified sampling or oversampling of very_hard patterns to ensure non‑negligible error rates; (5) enable repair invocation logging and instrument rollback latency as preregistered secondary outcomes to evaluate mitigation efficacy. Each recommendation maps to fields present in validator_trace and execution manifests (repair_applied, validation_before/after, difficulty metadata, provider_call accounting) and thus can be implemented and audited using the archived artifact schema.

Threats to validity and external generalizability. Model and scope: a single declared generator (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator were evaluated; results do not generalize across models or verifiers. Construct validity: reusing the same deterministic implementation for runtime guarding and post‑hoc scoring conflates acceptance and scoring. Environment realism: the benchmark is synthetic and the simulator/validator do not capture production telemetry noise, operator procedures, or adversarial actor behaviors. Adversarial robustness and human‑in‑the‑loop efficacy were not exercised; these remain open. Aggregation gap: the full per‑task difficulty labels are archived; we report representative examples rather than invent aggregated N=400 difficulty counts because the analysis artifacts do not contain a precomputed aggregate histogram.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on an action‑aware staging benchmark. Under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied the deterministic runtime validator and both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). This deterministic ceiling effect stemmed from preregistered design and implementation homogeneity and renders the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard interactions in this run. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and to support hardened follow‑on experiments (independent generation, adversarial seeding, heterogeneous validators) that exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors. The artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations provide concrete steps researchers can preregister to preserve statistical signal when evaluating runtime verifier utility in NetOps settings.

limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: the experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for future work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting gap: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and can be aggregated by auditors; the manuscript reports representative sample counts (first six tasks) to illustrate benchmark diversity but does not fabricate aggregated N=400 difficulty counts.
